speakeroldname: Mr. Harold E. Winch (Vancouver East) moved:
speechtext:
That, in order to promote the development of the highest degree of morale amongst federal civil servants through removal of obstacles to settlement of fundamental grievances and to enable official spokesmen to appear before a standing committee of the House of Commons, standing order 65 (1) be amended by adding a paragraph (o) to read as follows:
"(o) on civil service affairs, to consist of 35 members, 10 of whom shall constitute a quorum;"
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion which I am sponsoring at this time is concise and, I think, is self-explanatory. I am not too much concerned about the details as to the constitution of the suggested committee, the numbers or the quorum. What I desire to speak on this afternoon has to do wholly and solely with the principles and the suggestion

that the standing order be amended so as to provide for a committee on civil service affairs. I can assure you, sir, that this motion was placed on the order paper only after a great deal of consideration and after consultation with a number of the executive officers of the civil service association and after having been invited to sit in on meetings of the rank and file members of the civil service.
This is the fifth parliament of Canada, Mr. Speaker, of which I have had the privilege of being a member. During every session of the five parliaments that I have been here I have heard the members of all parties speak in the highest possible terms of the federal civil service of Canada. Time after time, the members of all parties have spoken, and spoken truly, of the high quality of our civil service. Members have referred to the sincerity of civil servants, their integrity, their ability and their loyalty. I agree with all these expressions about our civil service. Unfortunately, however, it has been our experience that these are only words, only platitudes, only generalities, because no action has been taken over the years either by Liberal or Conservative governments to express approval of the civil service in the form of regulations or procedures whereby their fundamental grievances or problems could be tackled. I am convinced, sir, that the time is now long past when we should express our gratitude to those who have the responsibility for carrying out the laws that are adopted by the House of Commons. These people are the public relations officers of parliament itself in dealing with the people. We should express our appreciation by showing them that we want to assist them in resolving their problems and difficulties. By our policies and decisions, we should make it clear to the civil servants that everything possible is being done by the members of parliament who, you might say in the final analysis, are almost their employers. By doing these things, we would maintain the highest morale amongst the
300,000	or 400,000 civil servants who come within our jurisdiction.
I regret having to say, sir, that as a result of the many matters brought to my attention by civil servants, as a result of my attendance at meetings of the rank and file, particularly the lower echelons of the civil service, the esprit de corps, the morale of the civil service is perhaps at the lowest ebb in many years. It is at a low ebb because of the failure of the House of Commons in general, and governments in particular, to take action to resolve the difficulties of the civil service or to lay down policies that would give civil servants a clear insight as to how they could
19, 1963	.1357
Suggested Committee on Public Service handle negotiations, how they can get grievances settled, how they can achieve a basis of understanding as between employer and employee.
I want to admit, sir, that amongst the civil service associations in Canada on a federal basis there is not complete unanimity. However, I think I might say there is a desire amongst the memberships to be first class citizens, and not second class, as employees of this country. They desire collective bargaining, but admittedly there may be some differentiation between associations as to whether collective bargaining should mean the same rights as other organized workers in Canada or whether it should be similar to the negotiations policemen and firemen have, that is compulsory acceptance of an arbitration award.
However, sir, those are matters which could undoubtedly be resolved and, from my point of view, might perhaps be resolved if there could be a discussion between a committee of the House of Commons and the official spokesmen of the various associations within the federal civil service. I go beyond that basic principle of collective bargaining. I say that the time has now arrived when, because of the inaction of governments both now and in the past to deal with fundamental grievances in the interests of the efficiency of the public service, there should be a change in our standing orders to enable us to have a standing committee before whom the official spokesmen of the civil servants could appear and to whom they could present any fundamental grievances. Then the committee, in its wisdom, after consideration could make a recommendation to this House of Commons and through the House of Commons to those who have the responsibility for the final agreement with employees of the federal government.
Without any question, they have grievances. Undoubtedly, one of their grievances has to do with working conditions and pay. Those of us who have been here over the years, and who have been here especially during the past two years, cannot help but reach the conclusion that there has been a government policy to the effect that to those who have more shall be given, and to those who have not, moonlighting. No official statistics are available in Canada on any of the categories of workers in our country, but perhaps there is more moonlighting amongst civil servants than any other group. This is not because they desire it but because in the lower echelons, and this covers thousands upon thousands, it is the only way they can provide for themselves and their families the standard of living to which they are entitled in Canada. This requires moonlighting by the head of the family or requires the husband and wife both
1358	HOUSE OF
Suggested Committee on Public Service to work. I was amazed, sir, to find, and to find conclusively, that many of those who work eight hours a day for the federal government then work four to six hours a night as janitors in supermarkets or office blocks. This situation exists amongst civil servants not only because of the neglect of this parliament in general, but in particular because of the attitude of those responsible for wage policies as they apply to the civil service. As I said a moment ago, to those who have more shall be given, and to those who have not, that is the lower echelons, the lower pay categories, only faith and hope.
I would like to give just one example, although I could give many. It is not directly a civil service matter, but the principle is the same. Take the most recent increases to the armed forces. They became effective on October 1, 1962. An ordinary seaman in the navy, a private in the army and an aircraftsman second class in the air force got a $48 annual increase, but if you were a captain in the navy, a colonel in the army or a group captain in the air force you got a $1,080 annual increase. And that, Mr. Speaker, was supposedly based on a policy to take care of the increased cost of living.
When you see policies of that nature applied throughout the entire civil service it is no wonder there is a breakdown in esprit de corps and morale.
This house has become very concerned when it sees any possibility of industrial disruption because of long drawn out negotiations. Just now longshoremen in Vancouver have taken a strike vote, and I believe around 95 per cent of them voted to strike. Over 14 months of negotiations they could not reach a settlement, and now this will disrupt the waterfront industry in Vancouver. But what about the situation of our federal civil servants, many of whom have been taking part in negotiations for two years and there is still no decision? The most damnable feature of all is that it applies mainly to those who need an increase most. As members of parliament we are to be indicted if we allow certain situations to carry on.
Take the case of postal clerks and postal carriers. Postal clerks have to have some education and undergo examinations twice a year, and sometimes three or four on-spot examinations. They must know hundreds of thousands of post offices and how to direct mail by the fastest route, but yet we pay them less than the pay of a street cleaner. I am not deprecating the importance of street cleaners. They are vitally important to all of us, but take the case of the postal clerk and what he has to do. How can we justify paying him less than a street cleaner? Then take the position of postal carriers.


Take also the case of those who are employed in this building as sessional staff. Even today the Minister of Finance stated he is not in a position to state what is going to be done. There are many fundamental grievances of this nature.
I have been making a study of some of the regulations that apply to employees who come under the authority of some bureaucrats in various departments. I maintain that a few of these regulations are contrary to the bill of rights. They are definitely contrary to provincial legislation as regards holidays with pay, as regards monetary penalties on being late for work, and as regards using a car at the end of a postal carrier route to get down to a district post office in order to check out.
It is quite obvious no action has been taken to correct many of the fundamental grievances that exist. There is not any definite policy. Take the question of wages. All the executive officers of the various associations to whom I have spoken just do not know where they are at. A few years ago, by authority of this house, we established a special branch on job evaluation, on a basis of civil service salaries compared with those of outside workers. A report was brought in, but what happened to it? The civil service might be prepared to accept it, but when it reached the treasury board they did not like the basis of the orientation and they brought in their own, based on nothing. And so the civil servants do not know where they are. I believe that was the main reason for the meeting on June 14 between the Minister of Finance and the executive officers of the federal civil service association.
I am just trying to outline our views that for the maintenance of the esprit de corps and morale of the civil service we should amend our standing orders so that, through official spokesmen, fundamental grievances that could not be resolved in any other way could be placed before a committee of the House of Commons for its consideration. I believe this would give a lift to the administrators and those men and women in charge of the public relations of the government.
There is one other point of this suggestion. The appointment of such a committee would serve a very useful purpose in that hon. members of the house who have things brought to their attention that should be handled by civil servants themselves, but for varying reasons are not so handled, could bring these matters to the attention of the committee.
Take, for example, our own security staff right here in this house. How can they bring up basic problems themselves? It is pretty difficult. The majority of hon. members can

5et away over week ends, but we who come from the maritimes and British Columbia are in the House of Commons seven days a week. We see what goes on, and it is a disgrace that we have a security staff which I maintain is undermanned by at least 10 men.
These buildings are the property of the people of Canada. We want the public to come here, to see the buildings and learn all about them. They do come here in their thousands. Have you ever been in the house on a holiday, a Saturday or Sunday, Mr. Speaker? Some days there are 3,000, 4,000 and 5,000 visitors, but we have a security staff so undermanned that instead of explaining the buildings to groups of 35 or 50 I have seen them having to cope with groups of 100, 125 and 150. It is not right; it is not fair.
It is important to let the civil servants know that we mean what we say about their sincerity, integrity and loyalty, and by our decisions we must show we believe they should be among the first of the first class citizens of the country, and not second class citizens denied rights and opportunities that are open to others. That is why I moved this motion. I hope it will be carried; but even if it is not, I trust it will be an indication to the government now in office, to the people responsible for policies and negotiations, that we are vitally interested in our civil service and we are not going to rest content until they get a square and decent deal.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is proposing that a standing committee of the house be set up to deal with problems and grievances relating to the civil service. When looking at any of these resolutions or proposals for legislation, I think we have to first of all ascertain whether there is a problem that needs to be solved. Second, we must decide whether this is the correct way to solve the problem we have uncovered. Let us look at this particular proposal in that light.
First of all, in talking about the civil service I am sure all of us would agree with the hon. member when he describes in the highest possible terms the quality, integrity and ability of our civil service. We all know that the civil service in this country has done and continues to do an outstanding job in carrying on the business of government. I think we must also realize that in addition to being a group of people of high quality, they are a very important group carrying out the business of government. From the straight point of view of dollars, looking at the estimates for this year we see that civil service salaries and wages amount to some $875 million. So we are not dealing with a small group of people who are easy to get together; we are
19, 1963	1359
Suggested Committee on Public Service dealing with a very large group of people. We are dealing not only with a very large group of people, but with a very large sum of money.
The civil service are important because they are in daily contact with the citizens of this country. Through their actions, ability and skill the public either have or lose confidence in the democratic process, in the government, because civil servants are the last outposts of government; they are the only contact that many of our people have with government. For this reason I think it is vital that the civil service be not only the best people we can attract, but that also in their dealings with the public at large they demonstrate that they are satisfied, well treated and happy in the service of the government.
The hon. member has suggested that our civil servants are second class citizens. I do not agree with him on that point. I believe they are first class citizens, but I also believe they have second class privileges. The hon. member discussed the problem of civil servants having to moonlight, not being able to earn enough in their jobs to support their families. I know this is a problem. I know people in the service of this government who are not able to maintain their families and have to seek outside jobs. This reflects on the efficiency with which they carry out our business, the business of the government. I know also that in the civil service there are grievances and that sometimes grievance procedures are cumbersome and difficult. I know it is difficult to get resolution to some of these problems. I know also that in bargaining for proper pay and salaries it has been a continuing complaint of the civil service that they have second class rights. The bargaining is difficult; it goes over a long, protracted period of time. They do not have the strength that outside employees have; they do not have the strength of pressing their demands to the ultimate through strike action. It is for this reason that something has to be done in this area. I agree wholeheartedly with those who support the idea that there should be proper collective bargaining for people in the civil service and that there should be compulsory arbitration in settling disputes that arise.
There are many, many problems for the civil servant, but I do not intend to outline them all. I am sure I cannot bring tears to the eyes of hon. members of the house, as the hon. member who preceded me may have done, in outlining these problems. I think it is sufficient to say that the civil service, as it is now constituted, has problems in getting first class rights that go with their position as first class citizens. There is a problem, and
1360	HOUSE OF
Suggested Committee on Public Service I think it is a problem that we must recognize. What, then, is the solution to this problem? There are many possible alternatives that can be adopted. We could have a royal commission and shelve the problem for a couple of years. We could set up, as was suggested by the hon. member, a standing committee which would deal with these problems from time to time, and not only from time to time but over a permanent period of time; in other words, as future problems arise a mechanism would be there to look at and deal with them. A third method would be to introduce little bits of legislation one at a time, here and there as we see problems arising. It would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that of these three solutions the one with most merit is that suggested by the hon. member.
I think it would be a very, very sound idea to have a committee of this house on a permanent basis continually reviewing and listening to the problems of the employees, in effect, of this house, of the people who are carrying into practice the policies and legislation that originate in this chamber. I believe this might be considered to be a proper parliamentary responsibility, to carry out our legislation not only through the stage of printing the bills but to also make sure that the civil service do have a place where they can properly present and air their problems. I therefore commend the hon. member for bringing forward this resolution and wish to state that I support it.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to support this resolution. The dilemma confronting every private member at this time is whether to remain silent and refrain from making remarks, in an effort to accommodate the passage of a measure in the limited time available, or make remarks such as I should like to make at this point. I was for some nine years a civil servant; I had the honour of being a national president of one of the three largest staff associations of civil servants in Canada. I believe this resolution is a good one. There is a similar resolution, No. 65, in my name, which is designed to achieve substantially the same purpose as this resolution. There are some differences, notably in terms of the size of the committee and whether it should be a standing or special committee. I personally support the right to independent arbitration, which I think should be spelled out in specific, legislative terms.
As a member of this house I have on occasions had to listen to the type of intemperate attack which the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) makes from time to time. I will forgo the pleasure of replying


to that hon. member at this time because I hope to be able to do so when he is in this house.
A new act came into effect in April, 1962 which was designed to do certain things for the civil service of Canada. As a member of this house I have received a large number of representations concerning inequities in the application and administration of this act. For example, a group of geologists engaged on an 18 months term prior to their getting Fh.D. degrees who did field work for a specified period were classified as temporary employees. That classification has been abandoned, but the effect is that this group of civil servants is deprived of substantial fringe benefits, which represents a severe cut in remuneration to them for no good reason.
I had an example brought to my attention the other day of a civil servant who got a promotion without an increase in pay. It was a reclassification. When the pay increases were announced they were made retroactive and the net result was that he got $210 a year less than he would have got if he had not been promoted, because of the way in which the salary increases were applied. The staff associations have carried these cases as far as they can within the machinery available, but then they get stumped. They meet a stone wall. I believe there has to be some type of machinery to permit an orderly examination of situations of this kind, and the establishment of a committee as envisaged in this resolution is a step which I can wholeheartedly support.
In the United Kingdom there is machinery for dealing with situations such as this. It has evolved over the years and it is usually termed the Whitley council. I have read the reports in Hansard of previous parliaments. Representatives of the party sitting opposite in the house-not of the group putting forward this motion-spoke on many occasions to say they were in favour of a Whitley council, but they did nothing to bring such a council into being. I think the time has come when we should proceed to a more developed stage of dealing with employees of the government of Canada and crown corporations by offering them machinery for more advanced collective bargaining, including the right to independent arbitration. To make this work we have to determine the proper bargaining agents and units, and this is not easy.
The association I represented includes various professional categories in all areas of government service. Other types of organization take everyone in a department and cut across professional lines. In some cases the bargaining units will have to reflect the patterns in which civil servants have, in fact,

been organized. This will call for elaborate examination in one case after another. I think it would be an appropriate task for a committee of the kind suggested to sort out the kind of rules which would be appropriate to Canadian civil servants. We cannot follow blindly the experience of the United Kingdom or of other nations, because we have evolved here a fine civil service with its own traditions of staff organization, posing some unique problems.
The committee should set itself the task of examining the inequities which exist under a new act which created a number of difficult situations, and it should attempt to provide an orderly channel for the review and correction of the regulations under the present act. Orderly amendments could be prepared which would spell out the means by which proper units could be established, and representation could be determined by those units. This would be the basis of independent arbitration procedure. I am confident this will meet with the support of all staff associations representing major groups of civil servants in Canada.
I think it would be a fine thing, if at all possible, for hon. members to give serious consideration to the establishment of a committee to deal with these matters. I cannot see any other way of dealing with them unless we can arrive at a broad measure of non-partisan agreement in terms of the objectives we hope to secure. We have taken great steps forward on the industrial front in the development of collective bargaining procedures. We have made progress, also, in dealing with employees of the crown. But here we have lagged behind, and private industry has led the way. Legislation has been more appropriate in the case of private industry and there has been a reluctance, traditional in many respects, to deal with this matter by legislative authority. I think, also, there has been a certain amount of timidity on the part of staff associations and the civil service itself.
We have a fine civil service in Canada, one of the best in any modern country in the industrialized world. We have some of the most dedicated men and women serving Canada in circumstances in which, sometimes, they take abuse in silence; they serve because they believe in what they are doing. They are truly Canadians and they are proud of that fact. They are in no way second class persons. Some of the ablest men and women it has been my pleasure to meet are in the public service of Canada today, and in many cases they remain in this employment at considerable personal and financial sacrifice. I think we are under a real obligation to take
Suggested Committee on Public Service steps to see that we do better than we are doing now to bring about a situation in which the rights of civil servants are much more in line than they are at present with those enjoyed in private industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
am pleased to take part in this debate, because as parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State I am interested in the welfare of the civil servants. I therefore commend the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) for having put this motion on the order paper.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to make the house realize the civil servants have not always had the opportunity of stating their grievances. I read very carefully the proposal to have the house form a permanent committee which might meet the spokesmen of the civil service commission and study the civil servants' grievances.
I listened with great interest to the mover of the resolution; he submitted grievances which really deserve consideration. Moreover, I think that we should examine the lot of federal civil servants who are not getting a reasonable salary on which to support their families as they should.
I know also, that several grievances have been vented in various divisions but were never submitted to the responsible authorities.
As a matter of fact, civil servants are, in some cases, afraid to complain about certain conditions or to express their dissatisfaction in a certain matter, because they fear reprisals or loss of advancement within their branch if their denouncing of certain conditions ever were known.
Mr. Speaker, since my appointment to the secretary of state department, I have had the privilege to receive, from several hon. members, complaints made to them by civil servants, and I must say that, after having studied some files, I found that several of those complaints were justified. I discovered an attitude which, under certain circumstances, indicated certain trends that should be studied seriously, and more particularly with regard to competition notices for civil service positions.
As a matter of fact, I received representations to the effect that some notices of competition seemed to have been prepared to measure. I also noticed that this did not take
1362	HOUSE OF
Suggested Committee on Public Service place with the coming into power of the new government but seemed to have been going on for some years. One gets the impression that in the case of some vacancies, the qualifications required are so well spelled out that it is a foregone conclusion that Mr. So and So will be appointed.
Mr. Speaker, I am not afraid to tell the house that this situation was brought to my attention on several occasions, first of all by civil servants in my riding and then by hon. members or civil servants from other regions. In brief, I think that a serious survey of the situation should be made in order to see how things are done in the civil service administration, because we must see to it that the government employees have better safeguards than at the present time.
Also, the matter of bilingualism raises some difficulties in the province of Quebec. For instance, federal civil servants of good faith go to various regions in the province of Quebec to put French speaking candidates through oral exams. I think that is another reason why we should study very carefully what is going on and try to improve the situation.

speechtext: Certainly.

Does the parliamentary secretary think that the government intends to put forward this year an amendment to the Civil Service Act in order to allow federal government employees to take advantage of arbitration procedures, as it has been requested?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the information of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, I can assure him that under a Liberal regime government members will call upon the government to take the matter under serious consideration. MONTREAL STOCK EXCHANGE 453 St. Francois Xavier street Montreal 1, P.Q.
Office of the President
June 18, 1963.
The Honourable Walter L. Gordon, F.C.A., Minister of Finance,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Minister:
The financial capitals of the world have just about had enough from Canada. Last Friday, the initial reaction to the budget was one of bewilderment and dismay. Yesterday, it was anger and scorn. Today, our friends in the western world fully realize that we don't want them or their money and that Canadians who deal with them in even modest amounts will suffer a 30 per cent expropriation of the assets involved. And their reaction? If that is what Canadians want, let them have it.
May I offer a few general comments.
1.	The entire series of measures aimed at discouraging non-resident investment is based on a serious error. In the budget address you stated:
"As I indicated earlier, it is the policy of this government to encourage direct foreign investment in new enterprises in this country on the basis of partnership with Canadian residents. While this type of investment is of great value to Canada, it is our view that non-resident "take-overs" of established Canadian companies rarely confer any benefit on the Canadian economy."
This is complete and utter nonsense. A non-resident take-over confers great benefits on the Canadian economy. We may not like it but that is not the point. The new owners bring the advantages of new technology, new research and development, new products and ideas which can immensely benefit the Canadian consumer and which will be denied him otherwise. The former owners receive funds which become available for investment in new Canadian enterprises or in government undertakings which contribute to the expansion of our economy. Even if they invest the funds abroad, we reduce the balance of our international indebtedness and the income in dividends and interest from such investment
improves our balance of payments by reducing the net outflow on current account All this is elementary.
2.	Underlying this series of measures is a misconception about the part played by shareholders. I quote:
"I suggest that a 25 per cent equity interest is in most cases appropriate to ensure that a Canadian point of view is always available when company policy decisions are arrived at. A smaller percentage would probably not be sufficient for this purpose. A larger percentage would be neither necessary nor in many cases practicable".
Presumably, you are counting on the Canadian shareholder demanding a larger raw material content, a certified list of fees and expenses paid to management, detailed statements of the subsidiary's export efforts, prices of intercompany transfers of materials and components, etc. A not very proud role is assigned to the Canadian shareholder. His contribution will be to badger, to harass and to torment management and the 75 per cent controlling interest. How futile and how unrealistic. Today, the shareholder does not care that much. If he does not like a company or its management, he sells his stock and quietly goes his way. A greater Canadian voice in the direction of subsidiaries will not be obtained in this manner. The success (?) of the budget depends on Canadian shareholders imposing their will on the majority interest, which cannot be done.
Canadians have been given the opportunity many times in the past to purchase shares in Canadian subsidiaries but the record has not been a happy one as the attached table, which the Montreal stock exchange filed with the royal commission on banking and finance, shows. If subsidiaries do make 25 per cent available and Canadian shareholders do not respond, are we going to solve the unhappy dilemma by forced payroll deductions?
3.	The burden of the 30 per cent capital levy falls, naturally enough, on those who have saved, have invested and have so managed their affairs that they possess property and investments of a reasonable size. It falls on listed corporations by virtue of the amendment to the Excise Tax Act and it falls on unlisted, privately held and family owned enterprises by virtue of the following paragraph from the budget address:
"It will be noted that this measure applies only to the shares of listed public companies

Measures are under consideration, and may be discussed with the provinces at an appropriate time, which will apply to all Canadian companies including private companies. I trust that no flood of sales of established Canadian concerns to non-residents will develop in an attempt to anticipate the further measures to which I have referred, in light of the declared view of the government that such sales are generally undesirable."
In effect, a family or individual, forced to sell a private enterprise to provide liquidity to meet estate taxes and succession duties, cannot sell in the best market if that market happens to be non-resident. In many instances, there may be no offer from Canadians or an offer far below a non-resident offer. The owner has to compare a nonresident offer minus the 30 per cent confiscation demanded by Ottawa with the best domestic bid. A family, unable to obtain a satisfactory offer from Canadians and reluctant to accept a non-resident offer with the attendant 30 per cent Federal confiscation, may, in the end, lose everything if an untimely death forces the liquidaton of their enterprise. There are interesting implications here.
Skipping the semantics, we can see that the securities sales tax is not fundamentally a sales or excise tax,-it is a tax on wealth, a capital levy. It is far worse than 30 per cent capital gains tax because a capital gains tax falls on an increase in wealth between two points in time,-between the value of the asset at time of purchase and the value at time of sale. This new tax simply expropriates 30 per cent of the asset at the moment of transfer. It is not a sufficient defense to say that the tax applies only in the special circumstances of sales of assets to non-residents. It exists and the levy can be extended in its application at the will of the federal authority.
Second, if the government is not concerned here with revenue (the unbelievable rate is evidence of this), the purpose of the budget must be to destroy (prevent) certain activities engaged in by its citizens. In other words, the government is using the power to tax really to prohibit the sale, by Canadians of assets for money to citizens of the United States, United Kingdom, France or other friendly powers. I am not a lawyer but it seems to me that legislation of this nature respecting property and civil rights comes under provincial jurisdiction and is beyond the competence of the federal government.
Premier Lesage, Rene Levesque, Paul Gerin-Lajoie and other members of the Quebec cabinet have repeatedly referred to the gradual erosion of the autonomy of the provinces. The creation of the new securities
sales tax, without prior discussion with the provinces would be difficult to justify at any time; it is unthinkable in the present atmosphere of strain and suspicion. It is a perfect example of the manner in which a new tax 'gimmick' can reduce existing sources of provincial revenue or invade a sphere of provincial authority, namely property and civil rights.
The forcing of increased Canadian ownership by the use of federal taxing powers creates two distinct sets of problems,-(a) the effect on existing subsidiaries and (b) the capital levy on future share transactions.
(a) By doubling the withholding tax on dividend payments and by refusing certain tax concessions to companies with less than 25 per cent Canadian ownership, the government is in effect describing 'good' and 'bad' subsidiaries. This raises certain questions in the applied art of discrimination.
1.	Are Dupont and C.I.L. 'bad' Canadian companies? Less than 20 per cent of their stock is in the hands of the public.
2.	If they raise public participation to 25 per cent, will they become 'good' Canadian companies and qualify for reduced taxation?
3.	If Canadians hold 25 per cent of the shares of these companies one month and then reduce their holdings by 5 per cent to buy bonds, do these companies become 'bad' companies through circumstances beyond their control?
4.	Abitibi and many other Canadian corporations, operate wholly owned subsidiaries abroad. Will foreign retaliatory legislation force these companies to spin off ownership?
5.	Does the government intend to offer 25 per cent ownership in the subsidiary of Polymer Corp. to citizens of France? Holland?
6.	Does the government expect further direct investment (which it approves, see page 18) to be encouraged to come into Canada by these dipsy-doodling and discriminatory methods of taxing profits and repatriated dividends?
7.	Does the government not expect other nations to retaliate?
8.	Will these discriminatory measures improve Quebec's chances of attracting capital from Europe?
9.	Will we not, in the final analysis, find our capital in the Ottawa printing presses rather than the capital markets of the world?
10.	etc., etc.,
b. The 30 per cent capital levy is designed to discourage take-overs but makes no distinction between ordinary portfolio investments in the country and actual take-overs.

As a result:-
1.	The liquidity, depth and breadth of our security markets will decrease sharply and we can look for a decline in the market value of Canadian securities. The Canadian investor will be the first casualty of the proposed legislation.
2.	Supply and demand forces on Canadian markets become distorted. Foreign buying will be discouraged and Canadian owners of securities will face a 30 per cent confiscation if they offer shares to a value of more than $50,000 in one day. This is not a large amount.
3.	The tax will create two markets and two prices for Canadian securities-one in Canada where the tax is applicable and liquidity reduced and the other in New York where transactions can take place among nonresidents free of tax. Thus the New York and London exchanges will grow at the expense of the Canadian exchanges.
4.	Arbitrage houses, which operate between Canada, the United States and Europe and bring great depth to the market, will disappear. They cannot operate on one side of the market only.
5.	Hundreds of millions of dollars of Canadian shares held abroad overhang the Canadian market. The Canadian exchanges will now provide restricted and discriminatory markets for these investors. The liquidation of even a small portion of these holdings would be disastrous to the Canadian equity owner.
6.	The budget measures will encourage Canadians to invest in American securities where the markets are free and non-discriminatory. Exchange controls are clearly the next step.
7.	Funds, trust companies etc. will hesitate to buy Canadian equities because the markets in which they deal will be reduced and restricted.
8.	etc., etc., etc.,
We will not lay the foundations of a greater Canada on a budget such as this. Since the days of the Marshall plan, the nations of the west have been working toward a greater economic and political unity. This budget will turn back the clock as we Canadians shut ourselves up in our own tight little corner.
Foreign ownership is a problem in Canada. You are quite right in this but this investment is not financed by foreign governments or inspired by desires to impair our political sovereignty. It is financed by the savings and investments of friends in other nations and is successful because of the initiative and enterprise that accompanies and manages their capital. The antidote lies in our own private sector as we strive to accumulate the savings to invest on our own account and to find within ourselves a similar energy and imagination. This is a long and hard road but we must remember that we have sought, relied on and lived with foreign capital for generations and cannot now suddenly take an axe to murder the record of trust and confidence that has grown up over the years.
Some day, a political leader will rise up in Canada and say to the Canadian people that the solution to the problem of non-resident ownership does not lie in the vote getting arena at all; only then will Canadians have found true leadership and only then will our friends abroad breathe more easily and be happy for us.
Sincerely,
President.
